facts.headline: The sculptor who built this statue was never invited to its unveiling
facts.body_html: French sculptor Paul Landowski built Christ the Redeemer's face and hands in Paris and shipped them to Rio in pieces for the 1931 unveiling — the statue gets struck by lightning roughly four times a year, once hard enough to knock a thumb loose.

facts.headline: This cable car system is the third ever built on Earth
facts.body_html: The Sugarloaf cable car has carried visitors up Pão de Açúcar since 1912, making it the third aerial tramway ever built anywhere in the world — riders still switch cars halfway up at Morro da Urca before the final climb.

facts.headline: This isn't a bridge — it's a 300-year-old water pipe
facts.body_html: The 42 arches of Arcos da Lapa were built between 1723 and 1750 to carry drinking water into Rio's center — since 1896 they've carried something else entirely: the city's last working tram, still crossing the top today.

Lapa Arches Rio tram Santa Teresa

facts.headline: This staircase took one obsessive artist 20+ years to tile — and he died on it
facts.body_html: Chilean-born artist Jorge Selarón covered 215 steps near Lapa with more than 2,000 tiles from over 60 countries, funding the decades-long project by selling his paintings — in 2013 he was found dead on his own staircase, and the cause was never fully resolved.

facts.headline: More people may have watched this World Cup final than were officially counted
facts.body_html: The 1950 World Cup final at Maracanã Stadium drew an official attendance of 173,850 — but with ticketless fans and staff included, estimates run as high as 200,000, still the largest crowd ever at a World Cup match.
suggested_queries: Maracana Stadium Rio de Janeiro exterior

facts.headline: The world's largest urban forest was planted entirely by hand
facts.body_html: Tijuca Forest was cleared for coffee plantations, then hand-replanted starting in the 1860s after the clearing threatened Rio's water supply — more than 100,000 trees went in over 13 years, making it the largest hand-planted urban forest on Earth.

facts.headline: Rio's Carnival runway was designed by the same architect who built its capital city
facts.body_html: Oscar Niemeyer, the architect behind Brasília, designed the Sambadrome in just 110 days — it opened in 1984, his first major work after Brazil's military dictatorship ended.
